item.title: Re: Sir Reginald
item.content:encoded:
I'm somewhat interested in a fictional character manifesting and having to deal with it's "unreality"

But the whole "it possesses people and takes over bodies" and "makes anomalous weapons" things seems less interesting.

My advice would be to cut out those two things and make him literally a physical manifestation of the fictional character, who at first is confused and then starts having to deal with the fact that he's a character from a tv show. That psychological conflict is enough to carry the whole article. The other two things would only feel like distractions.


Forum category: Writing Help / Help: Ideas Critique

Maybe my standards are low, because I can name more issues I have with this article than specific things I liked, and yet I can't say I didn't enjoy it. It's cute.

(Those issues, though, are that the pacing seems rather strange, an anomaly that regularly tries to escape did so successfully many times without explanation and without the Foundation really upping the ante, and the cat seems too easily swayed into not escaping anymore.)

Actually after I say that out loud, I think I'm gonna novote. Too cute to downvote. Too many issues to upvote. I approve in spirit but can't fully support in good conscience.

What makes you interested in this? What do you want the reader to take away from it? How will your story be told? As this, as it stands, is not even a monster manual entry… as it has very little substantive details.

item.title: Re: SCP-5640 The Stomach IDEA looking for greenlight
item.content:encoded:
I agree with Cybersqyd's perspective below… I advised tying the anomaly to the political story, but then you've gone and sorta used this political story as just background for a weird thing

I'm much less interested in a story about something some horrible government used to silence dissidents that is really just about the Foundation studying something… I think this would be better served with less focus on the Foundation and more on the horrors of the anomaly.

If this is about disappeared folks, that's a heavy narrative theme right there… don't abandon it to focus on testing with cows. The testing wouldn't be nearly as engaging as a discussion of how this government used something so horrible to enact its disappearances.

Finally… as Sqyd said below, because this is a real situation where real people died and were vanished by a government, you have to be careful. You don't want to make this just an entertaining story… because you're talking about a great horror perpetrated in real life. So I would suggest focusing in on that, and using the article to discuss it in a way that is meaningful.

item.title: Re: Incorporeal mass at the center of the Earth
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for the feedback. Some responses below.

+ Collapsed for brevity
- Close

If something was incorporeal in the core and then became corporeal, why would the core collapse?

It isn't simply more mass being added to the core, it is part of the core being replaced with the incorporeal objects, which are far less dense, allowing large amounts of additional matter to be pushed into the core in a large surge. it should also be noted that due to the nature of several types of intangibility there are several intangible corpse in a single place being expelled from each other while becoming corporeal, potentially causing large seismic disruptions due to the movement of large amounts of mass. As for the 'disastrous' aspect, that is what is being implied to happen in the scenario discussed at the end.

Don't do this, don't redact the size. It doesn't serve anything, do some research and figure out what sorta size you want to imply and just say it. Would be more impactful.

Fair enough, but what more impact would a unit of measure have? I am of the opinion that a well placed redaction can emphasize the horror of an article. To anyone who isn't familiar with the size of a human body or the size of the earths core a definitive amount I feel a definitive amount would lessen the impact. That being said, I may just blackbox the exact volume with a large amount of digits.

More of concern is the lack of narrative. There isn't an arc to this, its merely discussing the description of an anomaly. What is it you want to say with this article? What do you want the readers to take away from it? We can't really know what the people are going through as they sink to the center of the earth… so where is the human aspect of this anomaly?

You are correct in there not being a central narrative but for an anomaly of this type, there can't really be one, as it isn't the result of one central anomaly. The human aspect of this article comes in the form of the individual stories of the people down there, implied through their descriptions. Furthermore, due to the nature of certain types of intangibility some of the people are still alive and fully aware of there situation, but unable to do anything about it. Given that I am planning on having at least one of the people as a ghost, the foundation may be able to conduct an interview with them via use of a séance. Ending the article with the potential of disaster is meant to convey how this is truly a lose-lose situation, with them being stuck, us being doomed and neither party being able to do anything about it.

item.title: Re: How do Type Greens come to be?
item.content:encoded:
There's a bit of info about their skill progression here, from a GOC perspective.

The Hume FAQ might also interest you. It also has a lot of links to reality-bender SCPs.

Personally I think for your "standard" type greens, it's mostly genetic, and their powers develop as they age.

Alternate idea, in abnormal psychology we have a thing we call the diathesis-stress model, where someone might have a "risk factor" like certain genes, but this is only "activated" by a major stressor/situation.

However, IMO there are infinite possible sources for anomalies, so you might very well see someone else with nearly-identical powers that were given to them by a God, a deal with the devil, or radiation, or magic or whatever. It's kinda up to you.

Edit: You can also use Tag Search in the bar on the left and search for ontokinetic and humanoid to find relevant SCPs.

item.title: Re: Te Horoi Pai (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
I'm pretty lost as to why this anomaly leads to a disappearance… you describe it as a compulsive effect to spread the love for this product (summing up/paraphrasing) and then people vanish? Are the entities doing something to them?

Also, I have to say the whole "make a thing that forces you to spread it around so that hours later you're attacked by otherworldly entities" isn't the most straight forward of concepts.

Thematically, these entities seem discordant with a product that enhances a person's hygiene. What does that have to do with something representing "subconscious fetishes or extremest fears"? I'd also suggest being careful with the demonizing of "fetishes" because such things are subjective and often seen as "gross" from the outside but is in reality just another form of sexual orientation repression… Like a sexual practice you find uncomfortable doesn't equate that practice with extreme fear… suggesting those are interrelated is dicey at best.

item.title: Re: What award would somebody get for neutralizing a keter?
item.content:encoded:
Well, there's the Foundation Star, as shown here: SCP-1983. However, they were only rewarded for the neutralization given that this was an incredibly dangerous anomaly that was quite possibly impossible to contain and chewing up agents.

You could also say that readers didn't mind them breaking that "rule" because it was a good story.

IMO, if your story is about a reality bender being awarded for accidentally neutralizing a anomaly (which most readers don't think would be rewarded), and you're just picking between the most well-known Keters on the site, maybe read more of the wiki? That might be a hard story to pull off unless you have more lore to build from and know what current readers enjoy.

item.title: Re: Incorporeal mass at the center of the Earth
item.content:encoded:
Here are some minor quibbles with the internal logic you've presented:

+ show block
– hide block

causing part of it to become corporal before the unit is destroyed, causing part of the earths core to collapse in on itself, creating a minor earthquake.

Several things with this: a) If something was incorporeal in the core and then became corporeal, why would the core collapse? The core isn't hollow, its solid with liquified rock. Also, the core is made the way it is because of gravity pushing innumerable metric tons of matter into it, I can't imagine a little more would suddenly make it collapse even a teensy bit. More than likely that matter would then be vaporized by the intense heat and then some small amount of gas would escape the core potentially (but this is happening all the time). b) if part of the core were to collapse it wouldn't make a "minor earthquake" it would probably be disastrous.

The exact size of this mass is [REDACTED] by it is implied to be truly massive.

Don't do this, don't redact the size. It doesn't serve anything, do some research and figure out what sorta size you want to imply and just say it. Would be more impactful. Also in general, I am of the opinion that "redacted" information doesn't serve narratives in 99% of the case. Here isn't an exception to me.

More of concern is the lack of narrative. There isn't an arc to this, its merely discussing the description of an anomaly. What is it you want to say with this article? What do you want the readers to take away from it? We can't really know what the people are going through as they sink to the center of the earth… so where is the human aspect of this anomaly?

I think you should brainstorm concerning a narrative. Think about what sort of story you want to tell and come up with a way to tell it with this anomaly. Because at the end of the day, most articles that only concern themselves with "look at this weird phenomenon" don't do well. If you have some clever way to avoid using narrative to getting the reader engaged, I am not seeing it.

item.title: Realistic Portal gun SCP idea
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Horror, Drama/Emotional

Page Layout (Optional): Containment procedures, description, experimentation and recovery log

Elevator Pitch: There are many 'Portal' type anomalies in the SCP foundation, but never one that functions as a Gun. But what would happen if one existed.

Central Narrative: The anomaly is a stereotypical portal gun, that looks entirely like one from the game 'Portal' and functions as such. However, there are two twists to this concept:

+ Twists
- Close

1. Whenever someone makes a logical deduction about how a device would work, based on various aspects of science such as anti-matter or wormholes, the device will conform to that conclusion. For example, if a foundation scientist deduced that the edges of the portal would logically be superheated and produce large amounts of plasma, the portals will start doing so. The only exceptions to this are conclusions that would pre-empt the existence of the device or its initial functionality of shooting portals. These effects halt when the portal gun is deactivated. Eventually the foundation gets the bright idea to use the gun to create a generator, manned by uneducated D-Class, which ends in disaster when one realizes the portals violate the conservation of energy.

2. The device was recovered from a Level 2 reality bender. However this reality bender was also a quantum physicist and had built up an unshakable belief in the science, leading to the self-suppression of his abilities when they emerged. However the reality bender (hereafter called 'Bob') was also a fan of science fiction, especially the game 'Portal'. 'Bob' attended a sci-fi con with a model portal gun he had built himself and was discussion the possibility of making a real one in the future via use of quantum physics. Some of the other people at the con made fun of this, making him angry and temporarily un-suppressing his reality bending. Bob caused his portal to become 'real' and shot an actual portal, before realizing how such a thing wasn't possible. This lead to the anomaly in its current state. Bob was severely injured by the resulting extreme temperatures before the device was shut down by undercover agents at the sci-fi con. In hospital Bob writes a note about the clash between fiction and reality leading to his downfall before dying.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: A concept that would usually be placed in a -J article being presented seriously.

Additional Notes: I am unsure of the Creative Commons policy for game icons.

item.title: Re: Real Life Publishing Opportunities
item.content:encoded:
It means that your manuscript will be submitted without your name or identifying information. Your cover letter and whatever form you fill out when submitting the piece will contain your name, just not your manuscript itself when you submit it. This goal is such that if you are an incredibly famous author (or if you have a controversial name, etc) you cannot bias the editor in any way when they're selecting manuscripts. Certain editors believe that anonymizing manuscripts allows them to more objectively select pieces of work.

While I understand this may seem suspicious, please be rest assured that Diabolical Plots is a well regarded, SFWA qualifying market, and that if they do something untoward with your piece the reputation hit would be immense if other writers come to hear about it.

item.title: Re: Origami Brain
item.content:encoded:
frankly I don't know where exactly to take this to from here.

Figure out what you as the author want to accomplish with the eventual article. How do you want the audience to respond emotionally? Make someone feel sad? Feel hopeless? Feel frustrated? How would you want them to feel that way? By relating to the main character? By being invested in following the plotline? By being intrigued by the core anomaly itself?

I feel like the core of the idea is not landing with the audience here so there isn't much I can do to fix it.

By the looks of it, it's not clear to readers what the core of the idea is meant to be. Figure out the basics of what you want to convey with the article, and then reviewers can help tweak the anomalous aspects and the narrative to better present your vision. Better to involve reviewers in the editing process rather than just guessing on your own between revisions.

Please first go to the Ideas forum or the chat, give a quick summary (for the Ideas forum, please follow the instructions in the required reading thread) of the concept you want to write up (don't link the draft unless someone requests it), and reviewers can help you make sure that your core idea is something that will be successful with the community audience.

During the conceptualization stage, reviewers can also help by letting you know if something similar already exists on the site, and/or telling you if there are any cliches/pitfalls/other typical downvote reasons to be careful of with your particular idea. These issues are more effectively addressed earlier on in the writing process.

If you have already received the requisite greenlights, please note from whom and where you received them. If you would like to receive draft critique without going through the greenlighting process, please use the IRC chatrooms to request reviews.

item.content:encoded:
Hello! Before I give my critique on this, I would like to say that this is not how you present your concept on this forum. As per the required reading forum guidelines (http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/forum/t-13282684/required-reading:how-to-use-this-forum-ideas), you must fill out the concept template to seek critique. Go ahead and edit it by going into the "Options" tab then clicking "Edit" at the bottom-right part of your post.

Anyway, onto the critique. I don't find this funny. Aside from the fact that references to pop culture generally don't work, I don't see where the actual humor is. If the joke is that it's a meme reference, it's not going to work.

However, a knife that turns things into cake could work as part of the main series. Just add in some sort of narrative or something to flip it on its head, as the concept doesn't really interest me on its own. In addition to this, -J's are considered harder to write for first-timers, so a main series SCP could work out better for you.

~Koke

item.title: Re: Greenlight Concept - Article - Horror / History -Related to Sarkicism & CotBG
item.content:encoded:
Response to Critique
Thank you again for the help

Really my issue with this as a SCP is that 'the Foundation discovers the anomaly' feels too much like the end of the story than the start, and I'm kinda feeling like the history of the anomaly is the most interesting part? On the flip side, a deep, historical look at this could be very interesting if like, all the investigation is laid out; with the foundation assuming she's a new anomaly and then gradually piecing stuff together to the final ending where they discover who she was originally, y'know?

You and I are in agreement in how this narrative would/should take place, but I think it has merit as an article, with an accompanying tale.

The history of the anomaly is my prime focus. I've never characterized myself as a salesman, hence why an "elevator pitch" makes me nervous, but history is something I have a deep interest in and have dedicated my professional life to cataloguing and teaching. Perhaps I focused on the wrong aspect, as I am quick to discount people's liking of history outside of my own, and instead focused on the anomaly itself.

The extent of the article (still in brief) would be chronicling this SCP's existence over several hundred years, beginning with her discovery by the covenant. I was thinking that an accompanying chronicle of this covenant would be a good vehicle for detailing her existence, but this would be located after the fact and not immediately. The history between the Mekhanites and Sarkics is quite populated in ancient history and recent history, but the actual battles and struggle between them seems a little drowned out by the horrifying aspects of their dogma. This is an opportunity to show how their dogma and resulting rivalry produced a corruption perverse in the eyes of either side, and how everyone loses when they come to blows.

I'm not really sure what your addenda show, but I'm not convinced a test log would be that interesting here at all. I guess really what I want to know is how the narrative and the page layout tie together?

My thought on this, more explicitly, is:

I think there is a good way to piece this together and make it a compelling article, instead of a straightforward story which I think would allow for less intrigue. I've also considered the idea of making it so that the retrieval was an arduous process, and aspects of her were discovered during retrieval over a long period as she was tracked by a team. This would make it so that the article itself would detail bits and pieces of this entity which has a strange series of augmentations and behaviors, unravel bits of her further in the retrieval log, then tie it all together with the chronology (which would be incomplete/damaged) at the end of the article. Perhaps as well, a debate on whether to destroy such an item, exploit it, or keep it safe and hidden among different members of staff assigned to her.
